title: Two's Complement: How Computers Carry a Minus Sign
topic: Two's complement signed integers — flip every bit (one's complement) and add one to negate. The MSB becomes a sign bit, addition stays exactly the same as for unsigned integers, and a 4-bit register covers −8 to +7.

beats.narration: Computers only store ones and zeros — so where does the minus sign come from? Two's complement is the trick.

elements.content: Manimo bobs in centre-screen
Where does the minus sign live in a row of bits?

beats.narration: To negate a number, flip every bit, then add one. Take three: zero zero one one. Flipped: one one zero zero. Plus one: one one zero one — that is minus three.

elements.content: Bit row 0011, large mono digits in chalk
Step 1: ~ (NOT)

beats.narration: Sweep through every 4 bit pattern from minus eight to plus seven. The most significant bit acts like a sign — zero on the positives, one on the negatives — and the value wraps cleanly around at minus eight.

elements.content: 4-bit register with each bit cell in its own box; bits update live as the value sweeps
MSB highlighted as the sign bit (rose for negative, amber for non-negative)
Decimal value updating live, large monotype
Number line from −8 to +7 with a sliding indicator dot
Indicator dot on the number line tracks the live value
MSB = 1 → negative half. MSB = 0 → non-negative half.

beats.narration: The pay off — addition just works. Five plus minus three: line up the bits, ripple the carries, and you land on two with no special case for the sign.

elements.content: Horizontal divider line
Carry chain: per-column carry bits ripple in left to right
Result row 0010 = 2 — overflow carry out is dropped
the extra carry off the left simply falls away

beats.narration: Flip and add one — that one rule lets a computer subtract using only the same adder it uses to add.

elements.content: Flip and add one — and subtraction comes free.
(an N-bit two's-complement register covers −2^(N−1) to 2^(N−1)−1)
